title: Secular Jews
hookLine: Yiddishists, Bundists, secular Israelis: Jewish through culture and people

cards: A weeknight in a Tel Aviv kitchen. The soup is on, a grandmother is arguing politics with her grandson, and everyone speaks Hebrew, the language of the prophets, about traffic. Rewind the tape and cross a continent.

A meeting hall in a Polish city, a crowd singing labor songs in Yiddish, a school down the street teaching poetry and history in Yiddish too. Neither room has a prayer in it. Both are thick with Jewish life.
Today's word names the people at home in rooms like these.

teach.b: Secular Jews. Three groups and a book. The Yiddishists first.
They held that Yiddish, the everyday language of Jews in Eastern Europe, could carry a whole modern culture: novels, theater, newspapers, schools. You did not need a synagogue to be Jewish.
You needed a language and a people that spoke it. Then the Bundists.
The Bund was a Jewish socialist movement, and its watchword was a Yiddish word, doikayt, hereness: build a just Jewish life right here, where we already live, in our own language.

Other movements of that time gave other answers about where Jewish life should be built, and the arguments were fierce. Much of the world the Bund and the Yiddishists built was destroyed in the Holocaust.
What they asked survives. Then secular Israelis.

For some, Hebrew is simply the language of the morning bus, the Bible is read in school as the people's story and literature, and Shabbat is the day the family gathers, whether or not anyone lights a candle.
And a thread inside the Bible itself.
The book of Esther, in its Hebrew text, never names God. The people act.
Mordecai tells Esther that if she stays silent, help will come from another place, then asks: "who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?"
Rabbinic tradition reads God's hidden hand in that story, and the scroll is read aloud at Purim.
A secular Jew may read the same verse as a call to act for one's people. Same scroll, two readings, and the people in the room are all Jews.

how: Secular Jews often express their Jewishness through language, literature, food, holidays kept as family and cultural occasions, community causes and connection to the Jewish people, without regular religious observance.

o: Jews who have left the Jewish people behind them
Jews who belong through culture, language and people
Jews who pray at home but never go to synagogue

p: a whole modern culture in Yiddish
hereness: build life where you live

s: the book of Esther, in its Hebrew text, never names God
the people act, and Mordecai asks who knows whether Esther came for such a time as this.
the Bund's watchword told Jews to leave and build elsewhere
doikayt means hereness: build a just Jewish life where you already live.
secular Jews have no Jewish culture
Yiddish theater and schools, Hebrew daily life, songs, food and causes are all Jewish culture.

games.q: you're a Bundist in Eastern Europe, arguing with your friends about the future. where should Jewish life be built?
o: right here, where we already live.
games.why: the Bund's word was doikayt, hereness: a just Jewish life in Yiddish, where Jews already lived. other movements gave other answers.

practice: Choose someone whose belonging runs through food, language, music, jokes or a cause, rather than through prayer; it may be someone in your own family, or a part of you.
Notice one thing they carry that would be lost if they put it down: a recipe, a song, a phrase in an old language, a stubborn sense of justice. Let it stay in view a little longer than usual.

wordCard.voice: Secular Jews. Yiddishists, Bundists, secular Israelis and others who are Jewish through culture, language and people, often without religious practice. Today's word.

orig.note: Yiddish: hereness, the Bund's watchword for building Jewish life where you live.

carryVoice: Your line: secular and Jewish. A language and a people can carry a whole life. Until tomorrow.
